title: Jeremiah 6:1–15
context: Jeremiah 6:1–15 announces the siege of Jerusalem. The LORD tells the people of Benjamin to flee from the city, to blow the trumpet in Tekoa and raise a signal on Beth Haccherem, because disaster is coming from the north. Enemy voices are heard preparing to attack at noon and by night, and the LORD of Armies commands them to cut down trees and build a siege mound, because the city is full of oppression. He warns Jerusalem to be instructed before she becomes desolate. In verses 10–11 Jeremiah speaks, asking who will listen and saying he is full of the LORD’s wrath, and the LORD answers that it will be poured out on young and old. Verses 12–15 condemn the covetousness of all classes and the prophets and priests who heal the people’s wound lightly, saying "Peace, peace" when there is no peace. These verses appear again with small differences in Jeremiah 8:10–12. The location of Beth Haccherem is uncertain; Tekoa lay south of Jerusalem.

verses.text: “Flee for safety, you children of Benjamin, out of the middle of Jerusalem! Blow the trumpet in Tekoa and raise up a signal on Beth Haccherem, for evil looks out from the north with a great destruction.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the people of Benjamin to flee from Jerusalem, blow the trumpet in Tekoa, and raise a signal on Beth Haccherem, because disaster comes from the north. Arminian readers see an urgent warning that still gives people time to respond. The location of Beth Haccherem is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the warning as part of God’s merciful announcement before judgment. Both traditions note that Jeremiah himself came from Anathoth in Benjamin (1:1), and that the enemy from the north is later identified with Babylon (25:9).

verses.text: I will cut off the beautiful and delicate one, the daughter of Zion.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will cut off the beautiful and delicate daughter of Zion. Arminians see grief in the image, since Zion is pictured as a lovely and cherished woman whose destruction is a great loss.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as stressing the severity of the judgment on a privileged city. Both traditions note that some details of the Hebrew are uncertain, but agree that the verse announces Jerusalem’s coming ruin.

verses.text: Shepherds with their flocks will come to her. They will pitch their tents against her all around. They will feed everyone in his place.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says shepherds with their flocks will come against her and pitch tents all around her. Arminian readers see the invading armies pictured as shepherds whose flocks graze bare the land around the city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the shepherds as foreign rulers with their troops. Both traditions treat the image as describing a siege, which the following verses develop in detail.

verses.text: “Prepare war against her! Arise! Let’s go up at noon. Woe to us! For the day declines, for the shadows of the evening are stretched out.
verses.arminianNotes: The enemy voices say to prepare war, to attack at noon, and then lament that the day is ending. Arminians see the prophet giving voice to the invaders, which makes the coming attack vivid and urgent for his hearers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the enemy’s eagerness as part of the picture of judgment. Both traditions read the voices as dramatic speech within the oracle, not as words of the LORD himself, and they note the urgency of the scene.

verses.text: Arise! Let’s go up by night, and let’s destroy her palaces.”
verses.arminianNotes: The enemy voices say to arise and go up by night to destroy Jerusalem’s palaces. Arminian readers see the invaders’ determination, which shows that nothing will stop them once the judgment comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the enemy’s resolve as serving God’s purpose of judgment. Both traditions note that the palaces represent the city’s pride and wealth, which will be brought low.

verses.text: For the LORD of Armies said, “Cut down trees, and cast up a mound against Jerusalem. This is the city to be visited. She is filled with oppression within herself.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies commands the enemy to cut down trees and build a mound against Jerusalem, because she is full of oppression. Arminians see God directing the judgment while giving its reason: the city’s injustice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign rule over the invading army. Both traditions note that the siege of Jerusalem is later described in 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52, and they read this verse as the warning before those events.

verses.text: As a well produces its waters, so she produces her wickedness. Violence and destruction is heard in her. Sickness and wounds are continually before me.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Jerusalem produces wickedness as a well produces water, and violence and destruction are heard in her. Arminian readers see sin flowing constantly from the city, which shows how deeply it had taken root.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image of the well as describing a heart that continually produces evil. Both traditions hold that the city’s violence and injustice are the reason for God’s judgment.

verses.text: Be instructed, Jerusalem, lest my soul be alienated from you, lest I make you a desolation, an uninhabited land.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jerusalem to be instructed, lest his soul be alienated from her and he make her desolate. Arminians see a genuine appeal, showing that God still offers the city a chance to turn and be spared.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the appeal is sincere and see God’s warnings as a means he uses to call his people. Both traditions treat the verse as showing God’s reluctance to judge and his desire for his people to listen.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says, “They will thoroughly glean the remnant of Israel like a vine. Turn again your hand as a grape gatherer into the baskets.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says they will thoroughly glean the remnant of Israel like a vine, as a grape gatherer goes over the branches again. Arminian readers see the picture of thorough judgment, where even what remains will be searched out.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as stressing the completeness of the coming judgment. Both traditions read this alongside the promise not to make a full end (5:10, 18), holding thorough judgment and a preserved remnant together.

verses.text: To whom should I speak and testify, that they may hear? Behold, their ear is uncircumcised, and they can’t listen. Behold, the LORD’s word has become a reproach to them. They have no delight in it.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah asks to whom he should speak, since their ear is uncircumcised and the LORD’s word has become a reproach to them. Arminians see the people closing their ears to God’s word, which they now treat with contempt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the uncircumcised ear as a picture of a heart not yet renewed by God (compare Deuteronomy 30:6). Both traditions hold that the people are responsible for refusing the word, and they see Jeremiah’s frustration as real.

verses.text: Therefore I am full of the LORD’s wrath. I am weary with holding it in. “Pour it out on the children in the street, and on the assembly of young men together; for even the husband with the wife will be taken, the aged with him who is full of days.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says he is full of the LORD’s wrath and weary of holding it in, and the LORD says to pour it out on children, young men, husbands, wives, and the aged. Arminian readers see the prophet’s burden in carrying a message of judgment he did not want to deliver.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see Jeremiah’s words as showing that the prophet shares God’s view of sin. Both traditions note that the judgment reaches every age group, and they read the verse soberly, as describing the effects of war on a whole community.

verses.text: Their houses will be turned to others, their fields and their wives together; for I will stretch out my hand on the inhabitants of the land, says the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says houses, fields, and wives will be turned over to others, because he will stretch out his hand on the land’s inhabitants. Arminians see the loss of everything the people valued, which recalls the covenant warnings of Deuteronomy 28:30.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s outstretched hand as a picture of his power in judgment. Both traditions note that verses 12–15 appear again with small differences in Jeremiah 8:10–12, and they read the repetition as emphasis.

verses.text: “For from their least even to their greatest, everyone is given to covetousness. From the prophet even to the priest, everyone deals falsely.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says everyone from least to greatest is given to covetousness, and from prophet to priest everyone deals falsely. Arminian readers see corruption spreading through every level of society, including those who should have led the people to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing a universal failure of covenant faithfulness. Both traditions hold that greed and falsehood among religious leaders are especially serious, since they misguide the people.

verses.text: They have healed also the hurt of my people superficially, saying, ‘Peace, peace!’ when there is no peace.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they have healed his people’s wound lightly, saying "Peace, peace" when there is no peace. Arminians see false prophets offering comfort without repentance, which leaves the people unprepared for judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the danger of false assurance. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and note that the same words appear in Jeremiah 8:11, which shows how central this warning was to Jeremiah’s ministry.

verses.text: Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush. Therefore they will fall among those who fall. When I visit them, they will be cast down,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks whether they were ashamed of their abominations, and answers that they could not even blush, so they will fall when he visits them. Arminian readers see consciences hardened by persistent sin, which no longer respond to God’s warnings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the loss of shame as a sign of deep corruption. Both traditions note that this verse is repeated in Jeremiah 8:12, and they read it as showing that the leaders’ lack of repentance seals their judgment.
